description: We are Computer Science students interested in software development, AI, and space exploration. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to build an interactive educational game that lets students manage a lunar or Martian base. We welcome members interested in game development, programming, UI/UX, AI/ML, and space science.
summary:
AstroBase is a bilingual (Arabic and English) educational web game where players build and run a human base on the Moon. Players control an astronaut who collects supplies and crystals, constructs and upgrades seven essential buildings (such as habitat, life support, power, communications, and protection), and keeps resources above zero while surviving solar storms and meteor showers. Underground tunnels, cables, and pipes connect the buildings, showing how each system depends on the others.

The project makes real lunar science easy to understand. Interactive comparisons of the Moon, Earth, and Mars cover gravity, temperature, air pressure, day length, size, and communication delay. A weight calculator, a quiz, a memory game, and an AI companion named Robo, who answers space questions, keep learners engaged. All figures are drawn from NASA and Canadian Space Agency data.

It matters because it turns the abstract idea of living on the Moon into hands-on learning that inspires young people, especially Arabic speakers, to explore space science.
details: AstroBase is a bilingual (Arabic and English) educational web game in which players build and manage a human base on the Moon. The player moves an astronaut, collects materials and crystals, constructs and upgrades seven buildings (Habitat, Life Support, Power Station, Communications, Farm, Storage and Radiation Shield), and keeps five resources (Energy, Oxygen, Water, Food and Shield) above zero while surviving solar storms and meteor showers. Tunnels, cables and pipes appear as the base grows, showing that no system on the Moon can function alone. The game also includes a quiz, a memory game, a before-and-after slider, a weight calculator, and comparisons of the Moon, Earth and Mars (air pressure, temperature, day length, size and message delay). The project helps students understand what living on the Moon requires and how power, air, water, food and communication depend on one another. It also brings space-agency science to Arabic-speaking learners, who have few interactive resources in their own language, and it runs in any browser without installation. Published NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) science shaped the game design: NASA DONKI data on solar flares and storms inspired the solar storm event, NASA RadLab data on radiation doses aboard the International Space Station inspired the Shield bar, NASA OSDR studies on astronaut health informed the "Did you know?" facts, and the CSA food-production toolkit inspired the Greenhouse mission. The comparison figures for the Moon, Earth and Mars are drawn from published NASA data. In this prototype, these figures are stored within the game and are not yet retrieved live from NASA; NASA Mars Trek is planned for a future Mars level. The game was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single self-contained file, with the HTML canvas used for the game world, and it is hosted on Cloudflare Workers. The game illustrations and characters were created using AI image-generation tools and are labelled "AI-generated image" in our demonstration. An AI assistant was also used to support the development of parts of the code and text. The robot guide "Robo" provides built-in responses on four topics; open-ended AI responses are available only on platforms that support the Claude AI feature, and therefore, on the public website, Robo may rely solely on its built-in responses. No NASA logos or branding elements were used or modified in this project. The project is creative in that, instead of a textbook, learners operate a living base featuring an astronaut, the friendly robot guide Robo, hazard events, and a base that visibly grows with tunnels and lights, so that interdependence between systems is learned through play in a fully bilingual experience. Our team considered accessibility (browser-based, Arabic and English, simple on-screen controls), age-appropriate language for young learners, scientific accuracy, and transparency about what has been built and what is planned. The first level of the prototype is currently playable. Planned future work, not yet built, includes live NASA data feeds, a Mars level, and school activities using CSA resources.
